originalTitle: When bird flu hit the UK, suffering seabirds died in their thousands. Australia’s wild flocks will soon do the same
summary: Australia’s bird population will experience ‘large mortalities’ and risk species loss, modelling based on global outbreaks shows
content: Sandwich terns are a graceful seabird known for their committed, forceful and spectacular plunging dives into the ocean to catch fish. Thousands of the species started to fall sick across Europe in 2022 with tens of thousands dying as a lineage of the H5N1 bird flu – 2.3.4.4b – spread through the continent’s wild flocks. The effects of the virus on the brain cause the terns to flounder on the ground, craning and straining their necks in a suffering behaviour known as star-gazing. It is difficult to watch. “I remember a colony at Scolt Head Island in Norfolk,” says Prof James Pearce-Higgins, the director of science at the British Trust for Ornithology. “You had adult terns trying to mate with dead terns and chicks begging for food from their dying parents. “It was a real sense of a colony collapse as you watched this transfer of the virus between birds.” Sandwich terns are close relatives of greater crested terns, which are seen all around Australia and were the first native bird to suffer a mass mortality event from the disease in Australia on South Australia’s Limestone Coast. Since the virus re-emerged in Europe in 2021 it has swept over every other continent, killing millions of birds and mammals, and infecting more than 400 bird species as well as mammals – in particular, seals and sea lions. The virus was finally detected in Australia two months ago in migratory seabirds that likely brought the disease from breeding grounds in the subantarctic. Sign up to get climate and environment editor Adam Morton’s Clear Air column as a free newsletter This week, the federal government revealed analysis of the potential threat to Australia’s wildlife which showed almost 400 species of birds and mammals were at “high risk” or worse if they caught the disease. One expert who worked on the analysis, Prof John Woinarski of Charles Darwin University, tells the Guardian he expects the disease will have spread across the continent within a year. Pearce-Higgins says: “I would expect Australia is going to experience large mortalities, like those we have been through, and it’s going to put some species at risk.” Almost half of Australia’s bird species are unique to the continent, meaning that a lot of uncertainty comes with predicting what H5N1 could do to the animal population. It also means the risk of the virus causing planet-wide extinctions is higher now that every continent is affected. Death toll will be ‘confronting’ “We’ve been looking overseas since 2021 and seeing the advance of this virus,” says Dr Sara Ryding, an evolutionary ecologist at Deakin University. “It has been horrible overseas – tens of thousands of birds dying in single colonies. “The concern was, we knew it was going to arrive eventually – how could it not? But we didn’t know what it would look like when it got here.” Ryding has led research to project the level of risk from H5N1 for all Australia’s bird families by developing a model based on official reports of the disease from around the globe to the World Organisation for Animal Health. The research suggested the most at-risk families of birds were gannets and boobies (Sulidae), followed in descending order of risk by cranes (Gruidae), darters (Anhingidae), ducks, geese and swans (Anatidae), and gulls, terns and noddies (Laridae). But a host of other bird families – including pelicans, crows, ravens, falcons and kestrels – were all predicted to be susceptible. While many species of those birds are not considered threatened, the sight of large numbers of dead and sick birds, particularly larger species like swans and pelicans, “is going to be confronting,” Ryding says. “I don’t want to cause panic, but we have seen the devastation it has caused overseas and there’s no reason to think it will be any less devastating here,” she says. “I think it will be really bad.” Studies have identified several behaviours that can make animals susceptible to catching the disease, such as scavenging dead and dying animals for food (as do gulls and Tasmanian devils), spending time in dense colonies (like seals and waterbirds) and spending time around bodies of water where the virus can live for weeks or months, or where other infected animals might also be around. ‘Devastating’ for seals and sea lions The virus has been particularly damaging for seals and sea lions. Tens of thousands of seals and sea lions have died in outbreaks in Peru, Chile, Brazil, Uruguay and Argentina and, most recently, on Australia’s subantarctic islands of Heard and McDonald. The virus can cause debilitating conditions for the seals and sea lions – known collectively as pinnipeds – with severe neurological and respiratory symptoms. Australia has three resident pinniped species – the New Zealand fur seal, the Australian fur seal and the already endangered Australian sea lion – and government analysis has suggested the risk for all three from the virus is “very high”, meaning “very severe reduction in population size or viability is predicted” if the virus reaches them. Dr Saia Bartes is an Argentinian marine biologist who has just completed her PhD on Australian fur seals at Deakin University and has helped study declines in South American sea lions after the virus struck there. “It was devastating for them. In north Patagonia, we lost a third of the sea lions,” she says. Because pinnipeds often share space with infected birds, and tend to be in tightly packed groups, Bartes says they are particularly susceptible. Pinniped numbers are still recovering from commercial hunting, she says, and “they could start declining again really quickly, which is happening in South America” if the virus found them. Back in the UK, Pearce-Higgins says there is some hope. Their experience of collaboration with conservation groups, volunteers and local authorities through weekly and later monthly meetings had been critical in the response. chineseTitle: 当禽流感袭击英国时，成千上万的海鸟死亡。澳大利亚的野生羊群很快也会做同样的事情
chineseSummary: 基于全球疫情爆发的模型显示，澳大利亚鸟类种群将经历“大量死亡”并面临物种灭绝的风险
chineseContent: 三明治燕鸥是一种优雅的海鸟，以其坚定、有力和壮观的潜入海洋捕鱼而闻名。 2022 年，随着 H5N1 禽流感（2.3.4.4b）谱系在欧洲大陆的野生羊群中传播，欧洲各地数千种禽类开始患病，数万人死亡。病毒对大脑的影响导致燕鸥在地上挣扎，伸长脖子，做出一种被称为观星的痛苦行为。很难观看。 “我记得诺福克郡斯科特海德岛的​​一个殖民地，”英国鸟类学信托基金科学主任詹姆斯·皮尔斯-希金斯教授说。 “成年燕鸥试图与死去的燕鸥交配，而雏鸟则向垂死的父母乞讨食物。当你看到病毒在鸟类之间传播时，你会真正感受到群体崩溃的感觉。”三明治燕鸥是大凤头燕鸥的近亲，大凤头燕鸥在澳大利亚各地随处可见，并且是南澳大利亚石灰岩海岸第一种因这种疾病而大规模死亡的本土鸟类。自 2021 年该病毒在欧洲重新出现以来，它已经席卷了其他所有大陆，杀死了数百万只鸟类和哺乳动物，并感染了 400 多种鸟类和哺乳动物，尤其是海豹和海狮。两个月前，这种病毒终于在澳大利亚的迁徙海鸟中被发现，这些海鸟可能是从亚南极繁殖地带来这种疾病的。订阅气候与环境编辑 Adam Morton 的《晴空》专栏作为免费时事通讯 本周，联邦政府公布了对澳大利亚野生动物潜在威胁的分析，结果显示近 400 种鸟类和哺乳动物如果感染这种疾病，将面临“高风险”或更严重的风险。一位专家致力于
